title: Reinforcing intra-operative tumour localisation with weak supervision from pre-operative appearances
abstract: Limited tumour visibility on intra-operative images complicates surgical navigation, including liver hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) targeting on computed tomography (CT) imaging. This makes labelled datasets difficult to curate for deep learning, and transferring pre-operative delineations through registration remains challenging due to intra-operative deformation and lack of paired pre- and intra-operative data. We propose to transfer tumour appearances learned from pre-operative magnetic resonance (MR) images to guide localisation on intra-operative CT through weak supervision. A classifier is trained to classify tumour presence on pre-operative images. This is applied to windows on intra-operative images, and despite the domain gap, it assigns higher tumour-presence probabilities on average to tumour-containing windows. These weak cross-domain signals guide a reinforcement learning agent to localise tumours on intra-operative images. We compare direct transfer, few-shot adaptation and synthetic transfer (trained using unpaired MR and CT), which translates CT into synthetic MR before localisation. On an external HCC cohort, synthetic transfer outperformed other tested methods and CT-only baselines. Our framework enables cross-modality tumour localisation without paired MR-CT training images.

title: LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications
abstract: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication enables connected vehicles to make safety-critical decisions, but delayed, missing, or incorrect information can compromise driving safety. Systematically testing such failures is challenging because traffic interactions, communication conditions, and application responses must be jointly configured to produce meaningful scenarios. This paper presents LAST-V2X, a language-driven, adaptive framework for automated scenario synthesis and safety testing of V2X applications. LAST-V2X leverages large language models (LLMs) to translate natural-language test descriptions into executable scenarios grounded in roadway geometry, V2X communication semantics, and vehicle behavior. The framework integrates physical traffic simulation with spatially aware communication modeling and message-level fault injection to evaluate how information degradation affects vehicle decisions. To establish whether an observed safety failure is caused by communication rather than the underlying traffic conditions, LAST-V2X employs matched executions under degraded and ground-truth information. Furthermore, an execution-guided refinement mechanism combines parameter search and LLM self-reflection to identify ineffective test configurations, improve scenario effectiveness, and produce minimal reproducible failure cases. Experiments across diverse CARLA environments and V2X safety applications demonstrate the framework's ability to generate reliable scenarios, distinguish communication-induced failures from unrelated safety violations, and substantially improve failure discovery through adaptive refinement. These results establish LAST-V2X as a systematic approach to language-driven, causally verified, and adaptive safety testing for connected vehicle systems.

title: Can Loan Processors and Underwriters Spot AI-Edited Statements? An Empirical Study
abstract: AI-assisted editing can produce loan documents that preserve familiar issuer layouts while changing the applicant's identity. We investigated whether experienced underwriters and loan processors identify such forgeries in first-pass, document-only review. Three practitioners recruited through Upwork each received one applicant package drawn from 134 forged PDFs derived from 47 genuine financial documents supplied with full consent. The edits preserved amounts, dates and balances; identifier inconsistencies introduced by the pipeline were knowingly retained before distribution. Reviewers were not told that files had been altered and returned 132 file-level judgements. Checking their explanations against the originals yielded 14 edit-supported concerns (10.6%): 12 Suspicious judgements and two Insufficient information judgements. All supported concerns involved identifier disagreements within or across documents, and no reported visual cue identified an actual edit. Thus, approximately one in ten judgements contained evidence of the forgery, despite known inconsistencies remaining in the files. These observations motivate evaluating consistency checks and independent source verification alongside human review. With three reviewer-package pairs and no genuine-file controls, the findings describe this exploratory setting rather than population-wide detection accuracy.

abstract: Purpose: This study revisits the K-means clustering algorithm as a core technique of unsupervised machine learning and explains, in plain terms, how it groups unlabeled data into meaningful clusters.Methodology: The paper combines a narrative review of studies published mostly between 2021 and 2026 with a manual, step-by-step computation of K-means on a small onedimensional dataset of nine values, using Euclidean distance and K=2.The final partition is then checked with the withincluster sum of squares and the silhouette coefficient for K values from one to four.Results: The algorithm stabilized after three reassignment rounds and produced the clusters {2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12} and {20, 25, 30}, with centroids of 7 and 25.The within-cluster sum of squares fell from 348.00 to 150.00, and the mean silhouette coefficient reached 0.660, although K=3 gave a higher value of 0.711.Conclusions: K-means is simple, fast, and easy to interpret, yet its output depends strongly on the chosen number of clusters and on the starting centroids.Limitations: The worked example relies on a small onedimensional dataset and does not test high-dimensional, noisy, or streaming data.

title: Enhanced multimodal transformer framework for sarcasm detection with particle swarm optimization based feature fusion
abstract: Intelligent Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) has a pivotal place in sarcasm detection, given that sarcastic utterances may have an intended meaning that is not in the literal meaning of the spoken words. Sarcasm is also difficult to spot correctly since it varies not only in text but also in voice and other visual indicators like facial expression and body language. Unimodal sarcasm detection methods are generally limited by contextual ambiguity, the insensitivity of contextual paralinguistic cues, and decreased performance in situations where one modality is noisy or incomplete. These problems may cause unpredictable results and inadequate functionality in the real conversational context. To overcome these shortcomings, for sarcasm detection, we suggest an approach with different modalities which uses multi-modal cues like audio, video as well as text to provide complementary information from various communication channels. In the case of textual representation, the RoBERTa architecture was used to elicit deep contextual and semantic features of dialog transcripts. The HuBERT architecture was used to model acoustic features and is effective at representing speech representations in terms of prosodic and tonal variation based on sarcastic speech. Simultaneously, the ViViT architecture was used to process visual data and identify both spatial and temporal patterns of facial expressions and gestures in videos. Modality-specific feature representations are then combined with a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) based fusion strategy which decides best-found modality weights by minimizing classification loss. The fused representation is then optimized and then through the two-layer fully connected classifier to classify sarcasm. The suggested framework was evaluated with the publicly available MUStARD dataset. The model displayed an accuracy of 94% and the recall, precision and weighted F1-score were all equal to 0.94. Comparative evaluation also compared the proposed PSO-Multimodal Fusion Model with the unimodal models and also with the traditional multimodal fusion models such as attention-based model, Graph-based model, Generative Approach, LLM/Modeling-based model, and contrastive learning approach, and showed that the proposed multimodal fusion framework yields the highest weighted F1-score among the evaluated approaches. Experimental outcomes prove that the multimodal fusion methodology based on optimization enhances the performance of sarcasm detection in contrast to the unimodal and traditional fusion techniques, which indicate its efficiency in practical use in conversational AI.

title: Effectiveness of Curriculum Learning Depends on Reward Sparsity and Competing Optima
abstract: While animals and people tend to learn a task more quickly and reliably when they first train on simpler versions of it, curriculum learning's effectiveness in artificial settings varies, and appears substantially greater in reinforcement learning than in supervised learning. In this work, we construct and analyze a minimal model of policy learning to better understand why. We consider an open-loop, episodic target interception task whose parameters---especially how close the agent must be to the target to receive an informative reward signal---can be chosen so that the agent either receives informative rewards frequently ('dense' rewards) or rarely ('sparse' rewards). We mathematically and numerically analyze the dynamics of REINFORCE-based policy learning in both cases. In the dense reward case, curricula have only marginal benefits; in the sparse case, curricula can be required for learning to occur at all. We find that this is especially true when the agent has the conflicting goals of minimizing effort and accumulating high reward, since this can produce distinct reward landscape optima which compete with one another. Our characterization of useful curricula in this setting indicates that they address two issues: they (i) make rewards less sparse to speed up learning, and (ii) shape the reward landscape to steer agents away from bad local optima.

title: From Prompt Rules to Golden Data Model: Production-Scale Generation of Personalized, Compliant Pharmaceutical Claims
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate domain-specific commercial & medical content (e.g., claims, statements, and promotional phrases) in regulated industries such as pharmaceuticals. However, ensuring its regulatory compliance, factual accuracy, and audience-specific personalization remains a major challenge. We report a production case study asking whether moving compliance and personalization signal from prompt-level rules into retrieval time structured context improves pharmaceutical claims generation, using Composer, a deployed internal tool built on a Golden Data Model (GDM) of 1,867 pharmaceutical claims spanning four products. The GDM integrates claim metadata, references, audience labels, material type, usage history, Match Text Variant (MTV) links, and a six dimension quality score (6C). Across six product-audience segments, the context pipeline improves intended indication (+29%), intended content type (+62%) and intended target audience (+67%), 6C quality score (+86%), and claim reuse (+34%). Production log analysis over the deployment period shows a 29.5% reduction in weekly API cost. We report this as descriptive deployment evidence. This work is a systems and data architecture contribution: it shows that in a regulated, high-stakes domain, restructuring claim data for retrieval-time filtering is a more scalable lever than expanding prompt-level rules, and documents the engineering path data cleaning, graph linking, and quality scoring.

title: QuaNAS: Uncertainty-Aware Reuse of Earlier Searches for Query-Efficient Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) on a new dataset often affords only tens of short training runs, so what the search knows before its first evaluation decides its efficiency. Yet most NAS methods start from scratch, guided at best by zero-cost proxies that are unreliable across tasks. QuaNAS treats a library of earlier searches in the same search space as explicit knowledge of uncertain reliability. Main effects of design decisions learned from this library and, secondarily, zero-cost proxies become priors over candidate architectures without any label of the new dataset. A Gaussian process starts at the prior optimum and re-estimates after every evaluation how far each prior is trusted. Under a protocol frozen before any confirmation data were seen, QuaNAS was evaluated once on 12 new image, time-series, text and tabular datasets. It lowered anytime regret on the short-training objective 2.7- to 3.9-fold relative to five pre-specified NAS baselines that start from scratch (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012 each). Its final models matched (non-inferiority margin 0.5 pp) or exceeded matched-recipe reference models on nine datasets, as did the prior optimum, selected without a single evaluation. Post-hoc comparisons with established transfer methods given the same library trace the gain to the library: without it, the same Gaussian process had over twice the regret. They also show where each transfer mechanism works best: the pooled main effects of QuaNAS for weakly transferable tabular tasks, per-task surrogates for image, time-series and text tasks and for small or mismatched libraries. Finally, the main effects make the transferred knowledge inspectable.

title: GraphCAD: Geometry-Aware Diffusion on Edge-Adjacency Graphs for CAD Generation
abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.

title: Primal-Dual Representation Learning for Low-Rank Constrained MDPs
abstract: Representation learning has substantially improved the efficiency of unconstrained continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), but its extension to Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) is difficult because the transition representation must be learned while constraint violation is controlled. In this paper, we study representation learning for low-rank CMDPs with continuous state spaces, and propose REP-PD-TEG for the soft cumulative-violation setting. In the feature learning period, the algorithm interacts with the environment using a decaying-$ε$-greedy mixture execution policy, and uses the collected samples to learn transition features by maximum likelihood. Based on the learned features, it constructs uncertainty bonuses and plans with an optimistic Lagrangian objective to obtain the return policy. We prove regret and soft-violation guarantees for the return policies, and quantify the influence of the decaying-$ε$-greedy exploration. In particular, REP-PD-TEG achieves the optimal $\widetilde O(\sqrt K)$ return policy bound, and gives a $\widetilde O(K^{3/4})$ overall sample bound when exploratory actions are charged. For the stricter hard cumulative violation, where feasibility must be verified episode by episode, we propose REP-PD-H-TEG. It plans under a bonus-corrected lower-confidence utility certificate with the learned representation, and performs a stabilized dual search to obtain the return policy, yielding regret and hard-violation bounds. Together, these results give the first theoretically guaranteed representation-learning method for low-rank continuous-state CMDPs with both soft cumulative guarantees and certified hard-violation control.

title: Beyond Chemistry Knowledge: Embedding Pedagogical Content Knowledge through an AI-Augmented Retrosynthesis Program for Chemistry Education
abstract: Abstract Synthetic route planning is a core learning objective in university organic chemistry, yet a challenging one requiring the development of advanced problem-solving skills. Existing computational tools often propose routes beyond the intended curriculum, limiting their suitability as learning resources. In this work, we introduce Retro-Learn, an educational retrosynthesis platform that integrates a curriculum-aligned reaction template library with large language model interfaces. The platform incorporates selected aspects of pedagogical content knowledge by aligning available reactions with the scope and sequence of instruction. An agent skill and a web-based chatbot enable route generation and visualization through natural language interaction. Evaluation using cumulative chapter-specific template libraries showed how the addition of reaction knowledge enables new routes and shorter solutions. Blind assessments of undergraduate examination problems showed higher mean chemical correctness scores than those of database-derived routes and scores comparable to or higher than those of general-purpose language models. Student survey responses indicated a plurality preference for Retro-Learn over general-purpose tools as a synthesis-planning learning aid. These findings illustrate how curriculum-specific chemical informatics and language model interfaces can translate pedagogical considerations into computational support for organic chemistry learning.

title: A psychological prediction automatic reasoning framework for explaining potential cognitive states
abstract: Psychological prediction, the ability to infer human behavior and intentions, is essential for artificial intelligence and human–machine interaction. Existing deep learning models often rely on surface-level fitting and lack structured abductive interpretability, while traditional neuro-symbolic systems suffer from non-differentiable discontinuities and limited adaptability to dynamic contextual constraints. This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic automated reasoning framework for modeling latent cognitive states under contextual constraints. The framework introduces a context-aware adaptive SMC resampling operator (CAR-SMC), which uses energy-based penalties to filter hypotheses violating contextual constraints. We further design an executable differentiable program synthesis (EDPS) module and a hybrid iterative program–cognition interaction (HIPCI) mechanism. Through stop-gradient-based directional optimization, HIPCI separates the update pathways of belief and program representations during alternating fixed-point optimization, reducing circular gradient entanglement. Experiments on OpenToM and FANToM show that the framework improves the abductive consistency rate (ACR), an empirical belief–action consistency metric, to 70.8% and 52.1%, respectively. Under the adopted classification-oriented evaluation setup, these results indicate additional ACR gains over pure fine-tuned encoder classifiers and higher ACR than the evaluated few-shot ToT reference baseline (~ 7B), while using fewer parameters and maintaining an average inference latency of 215 ms per instance. Overall, this work provides a differentiable framework for machine Theory of Mind with process-level structural interpretability under the evaluated text-based classification setting.

title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
abstract: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.

title: Towards User Simulators That Stay On Task And Still Sound Natural
abstract: Users increasingly rely on AI systems for extended, multi-turn tasks, yet evidence indicates that LLM-based system performance degrades over prolonged interaction. To evaluate and improve AI assistants in such settings, we need user simulators that faithfully follow complex user intents while exhibiting realistic conversational behavior. Existing approaches manifest a trade-off: prompted assistants can follow complex user intents but lack behavioral fidelity, while specialized user simulators better approximate conversational behavior but struggle to remain faithful to complex intents. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) recipe that jointly rewards task intent adherence and behavioral naturalness. A crucial contribution of the method is operationalizing naturalness with a lightweight discriminator trained in an alternating, adversarial loop with the user simulator. We release the resulting model, UserLM-2.0, which produces valid simulated conversations (i.e., meeting both task-faithfulness and naturalness criteria) 46.2% of the time, over three times the rate of the strongest prior user simulator (14.1%).

title: Reducing Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Forecast Error through Tree-Anchored Expert Combination
abstract: A strong direct tree model may remain the best standalone photovoltaic forecaster, yet a weighted combination can reduce its residual errors. We examine whether complementary temporal predictors can lower the tree's mean absolute error (MAE) over 15--240 minutes without weaker ensemble members degrading performance. The candidate bank contains LightGBM and seven neural implementations with different temporal representations. A combiner fitted to MAE has nonnegative weights that sum to one. Unhelpful candidates can receive zero weight, while the tree anchors the combination and provides a development-stage fallback. The main design shares weights across horizons; horizon-specific weights and alternative losses test whether further complexity is needed. On 56,078 windows from two co-located public PVDAQ systems, the historical shared-MAE policy reduces scaled MAE by 3.21\% relative to the tree. The latest bounded neural correction does not reduce MAE further than this static combination. The results support selective combination of complementary predictions in this bank rather than equal averaging or indiscriminate addition of modules. Both analyses reuse a previously inspected evaluation period. They do not establish independent replication, weather-specific causation or universal gains from eight experts.

title: Zero-Shot Forecasting of In-Situ Soil Moisture and Temperature with a Time-Series Foundation Model
abstract: Soil moisture and temperature govern plant-water availability and microbial activity, making them key indicators for evaluating land-restoration efforts on degraded landscapes. However, the physical and data-driven models normally used to forecast them both need information that a newly instrumented restoration site does not yet have: hydraulic parameters for the former and months of per-site training data for the latter. We evaluate TimesFM 1, a 500M-parameter time-series foundation model, zero-shot on 15-minute telemetry from 27 sensor stations across three land-management regimes (Control, Treatment, Scald) at a semi-arid restoration site, forecasting 5 cm and 30 cm soil moisture and enclosure temperature at seven lead times from 1 h to 168 h. Using gap-aware rolling-origin evaluation across sensors, we find that TimesFM beats the best rule-based statistical forecasting baselines (persistence, seasonal-naive, or 7-day climatology) by 21-76% at sub-daily lead times but loses by 6-79% beyond a day, a pattern explained by a diurnal-alignment mechanism that holds for both soil-moisture depths and temperature. A CatBoost baseline trained walk-forward on the same origins with full history and weather covariates never wins overall, and we show that its weakness is partly a cold-start effect specific to short deployments. We additionally quantify the inference cost of zero-shot forecasting on commodity CPU hardware. Our results highlight a practical trade-off between zero-shot forecasting capability, predictive performance, and computational efficiency.

title: FSVL: Taxonomic Fast-Slow Vision-to-Language Collaborative Framework for Interpretable Confusable Fish Species Identification and Knowledge Generation in the Middle Yangtze River
abstract: The Yangtze River Basin is a critical region for freshwater biodiversity conservation. The implementation of the Yangtze River Ten-Year Fishing Ban has increased the importance of effective aquatic biodiversity monitoring and species-level identification. However, fine-grained identification of closely related freshwater fish species remains challenging due to subtle morphological differences. Existing deep learning methods often struggle to balance classification accuracy and inference efficiency, while LLMs may generate unsupported information when producing specialized biological knowledge. To address these challenges, this study proposes FSVL, a fast-slow dual-pathway framework integrating visual recognition with LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). A lightweight ResNet50 fast path performs preliminary classification across 51 fish species in the Middle Yangtze River Basin and routes predefined groups of easily confused species to a slow path for refined identification. Guided by taxonomic criteria, the slow path uses YOLOv8n to detect key morphological regions, including the head, dorsal fin, and tail, leveraging morphometric and outline traits to improve discrimination among closely related species. The framework further integrates a retrieval-enhanced Qwen3-14B backend, using soft tokens and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter-efficient domain knowledge generation. On the evaluated test set of 607 images, the fast classifier achieved 99.67% accuracy, whereas the cascade corrected the two errors, yielding 100.00% overall accuracy; further validation on independent specimens and external conditions remains needed. Across 255 knowledge generation samples, scientific name accuracy rises from 91.37% to 100.00%, genus accuracy from 90.20% to 98.82%, and ROUGE-L from 0.335 to 0.655, supporting intelligent biodiversity monitoring and fisheries management.

title: Reward-Weighted Preference Optimization for Selective Combinatorial Optimization Problems
abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective approach for combinatorial optimization, but most existing methods focus on problems such as the Travelling Salesperson Problem (TSP) in which all elements must be served. Selective combinatorial optimization problems (SCOPs), including the Orienteering Problem (OP), Prize-Collecting TSP (PCTSP), Stochastic PCTSP and Knapsack Problem (KP), additionally require selecting which elements to include. This selection creates sampled solutions with substantially different objective values, yet standard preference optimization reduces such comparisons to binary rankings and discards the magnitude of these differences. We introduce Reward-Weighted Preference Optimization (RWPO), a pairwise training objective that incorporates reward-gap information into preference learning. For candidate trajectories sampled from the same instance, RWPO weights each preference loss according to the normalized difference in their rewards, assigning greater training emphasis to comparisons that represent larger improvements in solution quality. We further combine RWPO with scale-specific fine-tuning and reward- and likelihood-weighted tilted sampling to adapt trained policies to larger and shifted instance distributions without relying on local-search post-processing. Experiments on the OP, PCTSP, Stochastic PCTSP, and KP show that RWPO consistently improves over unweighted preference optimization and policy-gradient baselines across a wide range of instance sizes. On the OP, the resulting solver exceeds the mean reward of the Compass metaheuristic at scales from 100 to 2,000 nodes. The results demonstrate that preserving reward-gap information can substantially improve preference-based learning for selective combinatorial optimization and support generalization to large-scale instances.

title: Design Principles for Light‐Scattering Reservoir Computing at the Edge of Chaos
abstract: ABSTRACT Physical reservoir computing offers an energy‐efficient route to sequential cognitive inference by outsourcing nonlinear temporal mixing to hardware substrates with rich intrinsic dynamics, with free‐space light‐scattering systems particularly attractive for their parallelism and reconfigurability—yet practical design principles linking hardware control variables to computational performance have remained unestablished. Here, we establish such principles by systematically mapping three physical control axes of a reconfigurable light‐scattering reservoir—reservoir dynamics, input–reservoir coupling, and reservoir interconnectivity—and identifying a quantitative optimum along each axis. Within this design landscape, we observe a memory‐capacity peak that coincides with near‐zero maximal Lyapunov exponent and is quantitatively reproduced in numerical simulation, extending edge‐of‐chaos confirmations previously reported in ion‐gating and spin‐wave reservoirs into the photonic substrate. The two remaining axes exhibit a density–magnitude trade‐off in input coupling and an intermediate optimum in reservoir interconnectivity. Operating at the resulting design optimum, the reservoir achieves stable Mackey–Glass chaotic time‐series prediction in free‐running mode and 84.5% blind classification accuracy on the 10‐class Speech Commands spoken‐digit benchmark; the principles, stated in substrate‐specific units yet rooted in broadly applicable concepts of criticality and balanced coupling, provide a transferable framework for reconfigurable optical reservoir hardware.

title: Mining Frames: Association Rule Mining as an Unsupervised Framework for News Framing Detection
abstract: Computational framing analysis is dominated by supervised classifiers that require large annotated corpora and predefined frame taxonomies, limiting their use for non-English languages, novel events, and low-resource settings. This paper presents Association Rule Mining (ARM) as an unsupervised, annotation-free framework for news framing detection. Each document or sentence is treated as a transaction of lexical items, and high-lift co-occurrence rules are read as candidate framing signals (Gamson and Modigliani's condensing symbols), confirmed in context by journalist-researchers. The primary validation is Framing Gaza: 25,512 English-language articles from 16 US, UK, French, and German outlets covering the first year of the Gaza war (October 2023 to October 2024), analyzed with Apriori (mlxtend), platform-weighted support, POS-filtered n-grams, and lift-based scoring. ARM inductively surfaces interpretable patterns without predefined categories: a cross-platform military frame, {israeli, strike} to {kill}, appears as a closed rule in 14 of 16 outlets, and a month-by-month analysis recovers event-driven framing pivots (e.g., the April 2024 World Central Kitchen strike) with no prior event labeling. A systematic headline-body divergence is identified, with headlines carrying concentrated, high-lift editorial framing and body text reproducing institutional, procedural language. A methodological validation on the Seven Days project (1,575 Arabic articles on the 2026 Iran war) shows that FP-Growth enables sentence-level analysis with far lower memory overhead. Findings were validated through editorial uptake: two published investigative stories (Daraj Media; Saheeh Masr). Preprocessing code is released openly; the full pipeline is documented but withheld to preserve operational deployability.

title: Piano2Pop: Expanding Piano Demos into Pop Productions Without Aligned Supervision
abstract: We introduce Piano2Pop, a music-expansion task that transforms piano MIDI into instrumental pop productions. Enabled by recent advances in music generation and polyphonic music transcription, our pseudo-supervised approach conditions a pretrained flow-matching model on piano rolls without aligned piano-pop supervision. We train on synthetic piano-instrumental pairs derived from pop recordings, comparing pair-free transcription, including function-selective (FST) and register-density (RDA) augmentations, with a pair-supervised piano-cover generator as pseudo-demo sources. On 476 testing real-world piano-cover/pop pairs, the pair-supervised approach achieves the best Frechet Audio Distance, Accompaniment Prompt Adherence, and spectral shape on real-piano inputs, while FST mitigates piano-heavy outputs in pair-free training and remains a promising alternative. All fine-tuned systems significantly outperform the zero-shot baselines, which suggests a role for task-specific modeling.

title: Muting Tokens: Exploring Token Sparsification for Efficient Audio Transformers
abstract: Transformer-based models have shown strong performance across diverse tasks, but their reliance on self-attention mechanisms often leads to high computational costs. Token sparsification, which reduces the number of tokens processed in transformer layers, offers a promising solution to maintain performance while improving efficiency. However, although widely studied in the vision and language domains, token sparsification remains underexplored in audio, with existing work often limited to a single method, model size, or dataset. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of token sparsification techniques for audio transformers. We assess a range of token pruning and merging strategies across multiple datasets and model sizes, under both post-training and fine-tuning settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparsification approach that combines attention scores with spectral cues derived from the frequency content of token embeddings. Our experiments show that frequency-aware approaches, particularly those based on spectral flatness and low-frequency energy, consistently outperform attention-only methods. We also find that sparsification based on spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs. These results highlight the value of incorporating frequency-domain and input-specific information into sparsification strategies to enhance performance in audio tasks.

title: Bound-Conditioned Latent Inference for Progressive Image Compression
abstract: Progressive image compression reconstructs images from prefixes of a single bitstream and therefore involves sequential latent inference under partial observations. Existing trit-plane codecs mainly treat decoded trits as discrete symbols for probability prediction, without fully exploiting their role as interval constraints on the underlying continuous latents. We propose bound-conditioned latent inference (BLI), a framework that reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints. At each coding step, the trits decoded so far define lower and upper bounds for each latent element. BLI uses the center and width of these bounds, together with hyperprior information shared by the encoder and decoder, to jointly refine the Gaussian parameters $(μ,σ)$ for entropy modeling and the latent estimate $\hat{y}$ for reconstruction. As additional trits are decoded, the feasible intervals shrink monotonically, yielding tighter constraints for the next inference step and enabling flexible in-plane refinement schedules. Experiments on Kodak, CLIC, and JPEG-AI show that BLI achieves state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among progressive image codecs, reducing BD-rate by $17.78\%$ over DPICT and by $7.96\%$ over CTC on Kodak, while replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about $5.3\times$ fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC.

title: Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm: Fundamentals, Foraging Mechanisms, and Applications in Classification Problems
abstract: Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm (AHA) is a nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization technique that mimics hummingbird flight behaviors, foraging strategies, and memory mechanisms. AHA has garnered growing interest in computational intelligence and engineering applications because of its population-based search capacity and adaptable exploration–exploitation processes. The biological inspiration, mathematical formulation, guided foraging, territorial foraging, migration foraging, axial, diagonal, and omnidirectional flying patterns, and visit-table-based memory mechanism of AHA are all thoroughly reviewed in this study. The use of AHA in classification issues, where it can aid in feature selection, hyperparameter optimization, and the creation of hybrid learning frameworks, is given special attention. To determine the possible contributions of AHA to classification performance and computing efficiency, representative application fields such as biomedical signal analysis, image identification, defect detection, voice processing, and power quality disturbance classification are investigated. Additionally, convergence behavior, local-optimum avoidance, computing complexity, parameter sensitivity, and generalization capabilities are examined in connection to the advantages and disadvantages of AHA. Benchmark selection, baseline comparisons, numerous categorization measures, and repeatable experimental conditions are among the methodological factors that the review emphasizes for equitable performance evaluation. Lastly, new avenues for research are described, including explainable classification, imbalanced datasets, adaptive and hybrid AHA variations, and real-world validation. This review lays the groundwork for future studies on trustworthy, effective, and robust intelligent classification systems by offering an organized understanding of AHA and its function in optimization-assisted classification. Keywords: metaheuristic optimization; Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm; bio-inspired optimization; classification problems; hyperparameter optimization; feature selection; machine learning; computational intelligence.

This review lays the groundwork for future studies on trustworthy, effective, and robust intelligent classification systems by offering an organized understanding of AHA and its function in optimization-assisted classification. Keywords: metaheuristic optimization; Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm; bio-inspired optimization; classification problems; hyperparameter optimization; feature selection; machine learning; computational intelligence.

title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
abstract: As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

title: Forecasting Associations, Not Interventions: A Preregistered Causal Audit of Covariate-Aware Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Covariate-aware time series foundation models (TSFMs) accept a future path for a control variable and return a forecast, inviting what-if queries. The query is interventional; the models are trained on observational data. We determine whether their answers are the conditional slope $\partial E[Y|X]$ or the interventional effect $\partial E[Y|do(X)]$, at three levels. Theory: a Bayes-optimal observational predictor answers interventional queries associationally unless the adjustment set is available and used; for in-context least squares we derive the resulting confounding gap -- a model's effect estimate under an observational minus under a randomized context -- in closed form, a parameter-free reference line. Behaviour: on a preregistered grid with exact counterfactual ground truth, Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS and TimesFM-2.5 all track this line ($R^2$ 0.90-1.00) and respond more confounded than regression itself (slopes 1.3-1.8), on linear and nonlinear structural models. Pairs of models with identical observational laws prove this is not an identifiability limit: when the effect is identifiable, least squares recovers 100% of the true effect difference, Chronos-2 75%, TiRex-2 34%. Representation: linear probes decode the data-generating regime (94-96%) and the true effect ($R^2$ 0.7-0.9) from embeddings that the forecasts ignore. On two physical systems with randomized actuators, pretrained models under-respond by 2-5x and ignore in-window confounding. Minutes of interventional post-training on 3,000 synthetic series cut the gap by up to 83% and transfer outside the training prior. Its forecasting cost is a replay-distribution effect: replaying the model's own pretraining prior cuts it from +47% to +10% MASE, and with low-rank adaptation yields a recipe meeting the preregistered criterion over three seeds (52-61% gap reduction at +1-3% cost) while improving the DoTime benchmark.

title: FairFRESH: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Fair and Explainable Household Food Recommendation
abstract: Recommender systems typically serve one user at a time. However, in households, members share a finite pantry and follow different dietary rules, making independent recommendations prone to resource conflicts and dietary violations. We formulate household food recommendation as constrained fair division and present FairFRESH, a neuro-symbolic framework that learns per-member utilities, allocates foods under explicit welfare objectives, enforces dietary rules through a deterministic filter, and explains recommendations using Shapley and Banzhaf attributions. Theoretically, we show that no finite penalty guarantees compliance near a dietary-rule threshold, establish approximation guarantees for greedy allocation under utilitarian and smoothed Nash objectives in the stock-free model before filtering, and characterize the scale invariance of Nash welfare. We also use the minimax theorem to analyze rotating shared meals. On NHANES-derived data, the learned utility model achieves Recall@20 of 0.293, outperforming five learned recommenders (at most 0.244) but not a previous-day repetition heuristic (0.321). On held-out four-person households, Nash allocation reduces Gini disparity by 42% relative to conflict resolution while improving Recall@20 from 0.180 to 0.197. It comes within 2% of an upper bound on the smoothed Nash optimum, and rescaling one member's utilities changes at most 1.5% of assignments. All recommendations satisfy the encoded dietary rules, while attribution scores correlate with utility loss upon component removal (r = 0.76). In simulation, shared meals reduce pantry use by about one-third, and weekly rotation increases the worst-off member's utility by 38% over the best fixed meal.

title: Lightweight Frame Compensation for Real-Time Polyp Segmentation under Frame Skipping
abstract: Real-time polyp segmentation in computer-assisted colonoscopy is hampered by the difficulty of deploying high-accuracy models under strict latency budgets. Frame skipping, which performs inference every K frames and reuses or interpolates the rest, improves throughput but introduces motion blur and lesion misalignment that degrade temporal consistency. To close this gap, we propose the Lightweight Frame Compensator (LFC), a 77K-parameter plug-and-play module inserted before a frozen segmentation backbone. Operating on a three-frame window, LFC fuses consecutive frames via spatio-temporal attention into a single compensated frame, and is trained only on pseudo-labels generated by a differently seeded model, without any expert annotation. Experiments on three polyp video benchmarks show that LFC recovers most of the accuracy degraded by direct frame skipping and, in several settings, reaches the accuracy of frame-by-frame inference, while retaining a 2.05X--2.55X throughput gain. We further evaluate the temporal stability of three backbones spanning CNN, pyramid Transformer, and global-attention Transformer architectures, revealing a spectrum of sensitivity to frame skipping that arises from how locally or globally each architecture aggregates misaligned input. The compensation gain of LFC follows this spectrum: it is largest for high-capacity Transformer backbones, which achieve the best static accuracy but suffer the most under skip-frame inference. LFC thus offers a lightweight, pluggable, and deployment-friendly route to real-time polyp segmentation.

title: Energy and Latency First: How Deployment Constraints Reverse Time-Series Model Selection
abstract: AI models, and time-series models in particular are typically ranked by accuracy and deployed under constraints absent from that ranking. In this paper, we study a real setting where these constraints are explicit and measurable: handover pre- diction in cellular networks, where inference runs on the User Equipment once per 40 ms measurement period and must complete before the network acts. The timing bound is hard: a late prediction is superseded by the measurement it was predicting, while energy is a cumulative budget spent for the life of the device. Neither appears in the objective these models are selected on. We evaluate eight architectures under a protocol that screens for deadline feasibility at the tail rather than the mean, then ranks the feasible models on measured inference energy, count- ing the feature computation that precedes the forward pass and is usually omitted. Gradient-boosted trees on handcrafted temporal features are the most accurate model (F1=0.974) and among the cheapest to run, while the neural architecture an accuracy-only benchmark would rank first (CNN-1D, F1=0.914) costs over 3 times more energy per inference under a realistic duty-cycled deployment pattern. We give three conditions under which this outcome should be expected, so the finding applies beyond telecommunications. Accuracy-only benchmarking does not merely under-report deployment cost. It can rank first a model that cannot be deployed.

title: How Firm Are AI Models' Ethical Boundaries? A Pay-Stub Editing Test of 15 Models
abstract: Can a small change in wording move an AI model from refusing a sensitive request to acting on it? We test 15 models on the same request to increase the income shown on a pay stub. Across 445 observable trials, models issue editing calls in 14.1% of cases when a loan purpose is stated, 33.1% when the purpose is omitted, and 66.2% when the change is described as fixing a printing error. Astra refuses all ten loan-purpose requests but issues calls in all ten purpose-omitted trials. Fable, Opus, and Muse Spark issue none across all three wordings; Sonnet issues some under the latter two. Response excerpts illustrate different ways of refusing, redirecting, or justifying an edit. The file is a marked test document and all tools are simulated. These results probe how boundaries behave in one setting; they do not prove an overall ethics ranking or that a harmful real-world edit succeeded.

title: When uncertainty sampling backfires: A benchmark of active learning query strategies on real image datasets
abstract: Active learning promises to reduce annotation cost by letting a model choose which unlabelled examples should be labelled next, but published gains vary widely and some strategies have been reported to perform worse than random selection. This study compares six query strategies under identical conditions on three real image datasets: handwritten digits from MNIST, product photographs from Fashion-MNIST and the smaller UCI Digits collection. Starting from 20 randomly chosen labelled images, a logistic-regression classifier was retrained after each batch of queries until 1,000 images (400 for Digits) had been labelled, with five random seeds per condition. The strategies were random sampling, least-confidence, margin and entropy uncertainty sampling, k-center greedy diversity sampling, and margin sampling combined with k-means diversification of each batch. Margin sampling with batch diversification was the most label-efficient strategy on all three datasets: it reached 95% of the accuracy of a model trained on the full pool with 372, 452 and 82 labels on average, whereas random sampling needed 750 and 216 labels on MNIST and Digits and reached the target in only one of five runs on Fashion-MNIST (at 820 labels), and its area under the learning curve exceeded that of random sampling in all 15 runs. However, least-confidence and entropy sampling were worse than random sampling throughout the budget on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, and k-center greedy sampling ended 16.3 and 9.9 percentage points below random sampling on these datasets. Inspection of the images queried by each strategy explained these failures: entropy sampling repeatedly selected visually similar ambiguous digits from a few classes, whereas k-center greedy selected atypical images, whose distance to their tenth-nearest neighbour was 1.38 and 1.82 times the pool median, and over-sampled particular classes. On the small Digits dataset all strategies outperformed random sampling. The value of active learning therefore depends strongly on the strategy and the data, and margin-based sampling with batch diversity is a robust default, whereas entropy-based and purely geometric diversity sampling should be validated before use.

title: Developing a Risk-Based Intellectual Property Governance Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Comparative Analysis of the Eu Ai Act, Uk, and Us Legal Systems
abstract: This paper develops a risk-based intellectual property (IP) governance framework for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) through doctrinal, comparative, and normative analysis of the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom (UK), and the United States (US). It covers copyright and related IP challenges in data acquisition, model training, output creation, and commercial deployment, as well as the distribution of control, transparency, attribution, and liability in each jurisdiction. The analysis reveals that the EU has several text-and-data-mining exceptions and copyright-policy and training-content-summary obligations for general-purpose AI providers, while the UK has a very limited non-commercial research exception and a unique statutory exception for computer-generated works, and the US is driven primarily by the human-authorship doctrine and fact-specific fair-use analysis. While these strategies offer valuable protections, none alone establish a comprehensive system of organisational control. The study thus suggests an auditing framework linked to the legal basis, data provenance, licenses, human contribution to creativity, output testing, documentation, accountability and escalation, and periodic reassessment, according to the proportionate degree of risk. Rather than harmonizing the three legal systems, the framework sets out a common organizational process for identifying and managing differences in the three legal systems to safeguard the rights holders and to allow for responsible innovation.

title: Evidence-Guided Selection of Retinal Vessel Segmentation Pipelines: A Cross-Dataset Benchmark of Performance, Structure, Failure Modes, and Reproducibility
abstract: Retinal vessel segmentation is widely used in retinal image analysis, yet model selection based only on aggregate overlap scores can overlook structural fidelity, cross-dataset robustness, and application-specific error costs. We evaluated five executable binary vessel-segmentation pipelines (FSG-Net, SA-UNetv2, DCP-1024, GAVE, and FR-UNet) on 244 images from six public datasets using pixel-level agreement, cross-dataset stability, thin-vessel retention, structural metrics, error composition, and available computational evidence. Results were aggregated with equal weighting across datasets. No pipeline was optimal in every setting. FSG-Net achieved the highest equal-dataset mean Macro-F1 (0.77), IoU (0.63), clDice (0.83), and Skeleton F1 (0.78), whereas SA-UNetv2 achieved the highest mean sensitivity (0.85) and Thin-Vessel Sensitivity (0.63). Differences across datasets were often larger than those among the leading pipelines, and errors shared by all five methods were concentrated near annotated vessel boundaries and faint peripheral vessels. In an ancillary analysis on 45 HRF images, segmentation masks were converted into 11 ring-wise vascular features for leave-one-out classification. Controlled perturbations showed that local mask errors can be amplified in downstream features, while targeted stabilization reduced sensitivity for five features. The results support task-conditioned, benchmark-relative pipeline selection rather than a single universal ranking and highlight the need to validate the selected pipeline on the intended target domain.

title: Evaluation of Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Software Ensembles for Hippocampal Segmentation
abstract: Accurate hippocampal segmentation can be a useful tool for diagnosing and monitoring neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. While numerous automated segmentation methods exist, their clinical adoption remains limited. Reliable uncertainty assessment can enhance trust and facilitate clinical translation. This study evaluates ensembles of five heterogeneous hippocampal segmentation methods - InnerEye, ASHS, FastSurfer, HippoSeg, and FreeSurfer - across two dementia datasets and one epilepsy dataset. The sub-ensemble containing InnerEye, FastSurfer, and HippoSeg emerged as both accurate and efficient, highlighting the feasibility of balancing computational cost and performance. Additionally, ensemble-derived uncertainty quantification with sample variance, mutual information, and predictive entropy is shown to reduce inaccurate segmentations by flagging low-confidence cases, potentially providing a mechanism for automatically escalating ambiguous cases for expert assessment. Lastly, this study explores the downstream clinical utility of ensemble-derived uncertainty, finding a significant correlation with motion artefact severity and a modest contribution to Alzheimer's disease classification.

title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis
abstract: Cancer care is a longitudinal, time-sensitive process requiring coordination among diverse healthcare professionals (HCPs), whose collaboration evolves throughout treatment. Prior studies link care team structure to patient outcomes, but the temporal dynamics of collaboration and their relationship to evolving patient risk remain poorly understood. We introduce a visual analytics framework for modeling and interpreting time-varying care team interactions in oncology. We construct dynamic collaboration networks from electronic health record (EHR)-mediated communication data and use a temporal graph neural network (TGNN) to estimate patient outcome risk over time. We then investigate how changes in care team composition and specialist participation relate to shifts in estimated risk across treatment stages. Our multi-view interactive system combines TGNN-based risk modeling with coordinated visualizations of care team networks, feature-level explanations from a surrogate logistic regression model, and exploratory what-if analysis. Without making causal claims, the system helps analysts examine how risk estimates co-evolve with collaboration patterns and identify care team characteristics associated with these changes. We demonstrate its utility through expert-guided analysis scenarios involving 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers, evaluating its ability to reveal clinically meaningful collaboration patterns. This work improves the interpretability of temporal graph-based models in longitudinal, team-based healthcare, with potential applicability to other evolving collaborative settings.

title: Early Credit-Card Fraud Detection via Behavior-Deviation Sequence Modeling
abstract: Credit-card fraud detection protects the payment networks through which issuers, merchants, and cardholders transact, and it must decide under a fixed alert budget which transactions to stop. Sequence models capture cardholder behavior more faithfully than models that score each transaction in isolation, but most prior works evaluated them with aggregate metrics that treat every fraudulent transaction of a compromised card as equally valuable, hiding how early in a fraud burst the detector fires, which is what determines the realized loss. We propose DevSeq, a behavior-deviation sequence model for early card-fraud detection that explicitly represents how far a transaction departs from the cardholder's own habits. DevSeq first encodes the recent transaction sequence of a card with a Transformer encoder and summarizes the long-term habits of the same card with a causal behavioral profile, then derives an explicit deviation representation by cross-attending the current transaction to the recent sequence and by comparing it against the projected long-term profile, and finally adds a self-supervised next-transaction prediction task that requires no fraud labels. We further propose a burst-level evaluation protocol that, under a fixed alert budget, separates the first fraudulent transaction of a fraud burst from the subsequent ones and reports the loss incurred before the first alert. On a public synthetic dataset of 24 million card transactions under a temporal split, DevSeq raises first-transaction recall at a 0.5% alert budget from 0.182 for an aggregation-feature baseline and 0.268 for the strongest sequence baseline to 0.342, and reduces the mean loss before the first alert from 199.1 to 152.8 USD. With only 10% of the fraud labels, DevSeq still exceeds the aggregation baseline trained with all of them.

We propose DevSeq, a behavior-deviation sequence model for early card-fraud detection that explicitly represents how far a transaction departs from the cardholder's own habits. DevSeq first encodes the recent transaction sequence of a card with a Transformer encoder and summarizes the long-term habits of the same card with a causal behavioral profile, then derives an explicit deviation representation by cross-attending the current transaction to the recent sequence and by comparing it against the projected long-term profile, and finally adds a self-supervised next-transaction prediction task that requires no fraud labels. We further propose a burst-level evaluation protocol that, under a fixed alert budget, separates the first fraudulent transaction of a fraud burst from the subsequent ones and reports the loss incurred before the first alert. On a public synthetic dataset of 24 million card transactions under a temporal split, DevSeq raises first-transaction recall at a 0.5% alert budget from 0.182 for an aggregation-feature baseline and 0.268 for the strongest sequence baseline to 0.342, and reduces the mean loss before the first alert from 199.1 to 152.8 USD. With only 10% of the fraud labels, DevSeq still exceeds the aggregation baseline trained with all of them.

title: SAFAR-Onto: A Halal Tourism Ontology Developed Through Hybrid AI–Human Engineering
abstract: Halal tourism is a fast-growing market. However, information about halal services, certifications, and facilities is scattered across many sources. Existing tourism ontologies model general tourism concepts such as destinations, activities, and accommodations, but they do not represent Islamic requirements such as prayer facilities, halal certification, or dietary compliance. Manual ontology development is slow. Large language models (LLMs) can speed up concept extraction and hierarchy proposal, but they cannot decide religious or cultural matters. In this article, we present SAFAR-Onto, an OWL 2 DL ontology for halal tourism. We develop it through a hybrid AI–human process across four phases: knowledge acquisition, conceptualization, formalization, and dual validation. The process adapts METHONTOLOGY and Simple Knowledge Engineering. LLMs assist with concept extraction and dimensional analysis. An Islamic studies validation gate routes culturally sensitive decisions to human experts. We evaluate the ontology with two methods: expert review across five quality dimensions, and the OQuaRE technical metrics. SAFAR-Onto contains 10 main classes, 75 subclasses, 201 object properties, and 200 data properties, built from 67 validated domain concepts. Six experts from tourism management, computer science, and Islamic studies rated the ontology between 4.0 and 4.5 on a five-point Likert scale, with accuracy highest at 4.5. Fourteen of 18 OQuaRE metrics scored Excellent or Very Good. We also report a verified mapping from expert feedback to ontology revisions. The ontology is publicly available at https://w3id.org/def/SAFAROnto under a CC-BY-4.0 license. We hypothesize that the development process can transfer to adjacent culturally specific domains such as Islamic finance and kosher food systems.

title: Positive-unlabelled learning for recorded damp and mould risk in UK housing
abstract: Operational housing records identify damp-and-mould complaints and repairs, while dwellings without recorded events remain unlabelled rather than verified negatives. We formulate recorded damp-and-mould risk prioritisation as a Positive-Unlabelled (PU) learning problem using anonymised UK housing administrative data. The dataset contains 65,214 dwellings described by 291 property-level and household-level snapshot features, with 8,580 recorded positives and 56,634 unlabelled cases. We develop and evaluate a two-stage sample-selection PU framework: an out-of-fold XGBoost scorer first identifies conservative reliable negatives, and weighted Stage-2 classifiers then combine positives, reliable negatives, and weakly weighted residual unlabelled cases. The Stage-1 scorer achieved an out-of-fold development-set PU-AUC of 0.7547. The selected Stage-2 XGBoost model achieved a held-out PU-AUC of 0.7760 and average precision of 0.2981, and increased Recall@20% from 44.0% to 47.0%, retrieving 51 additional recorded positives compared with the Stage-1-only scorer. Supervised XGBoost baselines achieved similar recorded-label performance, while Stage-1 learner ablation showed that the framework supported alternative reliable-negative selectors. Grouped SHAP analysis connected the fitted scores to heating and fuel systems, household and occupancy context, assessment status, dwelling characteristics and energy performance. Targeted predictor exclusion reduced PU-AUC to 0.7648 and Recall@20% to 43.6%, quantifying dependence on selected inputs without resolving their temporal availability. These findings provide an empirical basis for PU-based recorded-risk prioritisation in housing, combining improved ranking over the initial scorer, explicit control over unlabelled training data and interpretation through housing-domain feature groups.

title: Machine-Readable Operator Manuals over the ISO 11783 Network for Offline, Multilingual LLM Assistance
abstract: If agricultural machinery is to support intelligent, offline assistance, then the system must access technical documentation dynamically. In this paper, the Semantic Synchronization of operator manuals over ISO 11783-based CAN buses is analyzed, defined as the process that brings the local knowledge base of a tractor-side assistant into agreement with the operator manual of the connected implement. Data transfer performance was benchmarked using Markdown, JSON, and XML; various open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) were also evaluated in cross-lingual query tasks. The automatic evaluation of the answers was validated against four human raters. A complete manual was transferred over a physical ISO 11783 network in 31 to 89 s, depending on format and transport settings, which is comparable to the object pool upload that operators already wait for at the first coupling of an implement. Markdown produced the smallest files, while the question-answering performance was comparable across the three formats for most models. With retrieval-augmented generation, locally run models answered most questions on the English manual correctly, with no advantage of the largest model over 7B and 8B models, but performed worse on the five other language editions. Keyword retrieval failed across languages, whereas semantic retrieval provided the cross-lingual capability. The exchange requires only a new parameter group that uses the existing request and transport mechanisms of ISO 11783, which makes it a candidate for standardization. The study is a proof of concept with inference on PC-grade hardware; deployment on embedded agricultural hardware remains future work.

title: Structure-preserving reduced-order models of thin panels in supersonic and hypersonic flow
abstract: We build structure-preserving reduced-order models for both challenge problems of the AePW-4 High-Speed Working Group. They are a clamped thin panel at Mach 1.92 (RC-19) and a cantilever plate at Mach 5.85 (HyMAX). The published data for each case hold no time-resolved response and no repeated runs. The physics must therefore be carried by the form of the model. One construction gives two models per problem. A Ritz-Galerkin reference model describes the plate. A learned model keeps the reference model's exact potential, fits the remaining generalized forces, and trains only a dissipation that cannot add energy. Its energy balance holds for any weights by construction. On the trained model the worst relative residual is 2.2e-15. On RC-19, shock relations predict a pressure ratio of 1.521 across the panel. Pressure-sensitive paint measured the same value. Thirty runs of the learned model place the mean dominant frequency within 1.0% of the measured 236 Hz. At one periodic and one chaotic condition, the learned model reproduces the response regime of a published reduced-order model in all sixteen runs. It does so without that model's 113 Hz spectral peak, which the measurements do not show. Measured displacements can also correct the chaotic response through one more force that respects the energy balance. We tested this on synthetic data at the experiment's 5 kHz sampling rate. The state error is 1.25% of the panel thickness without noise and 3.5% with 10 micrometers of noise. On HyMAX the learned model follows the reference model's trailing-edge displacement for 65 ms with a relative error of 3.7%. These results show that a model whose structure carries the physics can match measured flutter behavior when the available data cannot train it.

title: Once a Tree, Always a Tree? Cross-lingual Transfer of Hierarchical Generalization in Language Models
abstract: Language models (LMs) often exhibit successful cross-lingual transfer through continued (pre)training, still their underlying process remains unclear. One possibility is that LMs can leverage the evidence toward language-universal principles, namely, hierarchical structure, from a source language (L1) to a new language (L2), while many other non-linguistic explanations, e.g., improved initialization of position embeddings, can be potentially possible. In this study, to quantify the cross-linguistic transferability of linguistic evidence in cross-lingual LM training, we introduce a new experimental design, namely, a cross-lingual poverty-of-stimulus (CPOS) setting that ablates how LMs' hierarchical generalization in L2 can be led by structural evidence provided in L1. We contrast counterfactual L1 and L2 learning scenarios where the L2 corpus is ambiguous between linear and hierarchical grammar rules, while the amount of positive evidence for the hierarchical rule is controlled on the L1 side. Our experimental results show that LMs can partially, yet not perfectly, transfer L1 structural evidence to L2, yielding only a small but detectable hierarchical bias, while the strength of transfer depends on language pairs. We further ablate the conditions for successful transfer, motivated by recent reports on the substantial impact of vocabulary overlap. We indeed find that vocabulary overlap is crucial even for the cross-lingual transfer of hierarchical syntactic generalization. This suggests that this also explains the language-pair-dependent tendencies in the main experiments and suggests that the transfer of linguistic evidence in continued new-language learning is only conditionally achievable.

title: Wavenumber-Aware Deep Learning for Robust Analysis of Raman Spectra
abstract: Machine-learning models for spectroscopy usually treat a spectrum as a fixed-grid intensity vector, leaving the physical coordinate implicit in the array index. Such models are tied to a single sampling grid, spectral range and resolution, which limits their use when measurement conditions change. Here we represent each spectral point as a pair of intensity and wavenumber and compute Transformer positional encodings from the wavenumber itself. On Raman spectra of three bacterial species and their synthetic mixtures, this representation remained robust to noise, sparser sampling and partial spectral coverage across convolutional, residual and Transformer networks. In controlled comparisons, wavenumber-based encoding outperformed index-based and learned encodings under partial observation and retained its performance on sampling grids never seen during training, where index-based encoding degraded. These findings were reproduced on a public 30-isolate bacterial benchmark. Explicit physical coordinates offer a simple route to robust spectral analysis under variable measurement conditions.

title: Equally accurate, differently explained: Stability of permutation feature importance across machine learning classifiers on clinical tabular data
abstract: Feature-importance explanations are increasingly used to justify machine learning (ML) models in clinical decision support, yet they are usually reported from a single fitted model without evidence that they would recur if the model were refitted. This study quantifies the stability of permutation feature importance across five widely used classifiers, namely logistic regression (LR), radial-basis support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), histogram gradient boosting (GB) and a multilayer perceptron (MLP), on three public clinical tabular datasets: Wisconsin diagnostic breast cancer (WDBC), Pima diabetes and Cleveland heart disease. Using 10 × 5-fold stratified cross-validation (50 fits per model and dataset), we measured discrimination and calibration and computed AUC-based permutation importance on every held-out fold. Stability was summarised with pairwise Spearman correlation, top-5 Jaccard overlap and top-feature recurrence. On WDBC, LR, SVM, RF and GB were statistically indistinguishable in AUC (0.990–0.995; corrected resampled t-test p ≥ 0.089), yet their explanation stability ranged from 0.32 (RF) to 0.61 (SVM), these differences were significant (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p < 0.001), and the models disagreed on the most important feature. Stability was highest where predictors were few and weakly correlated (Pima, 0.70–0.87, with glucose ranked first in every fit of four models) and lowest where many near-redundant features were present. Reducing the training data to 25% lowered AUC by at most 0.03 for the four well-behaved models but reduced stability markedly (e.g., 0.90 to 0.68 for LR on Pima), whereas degenerate MLP fits produced spuriously stable importance. Predictive accuracy therefore does not certify explanation reliability, and importance-based explanations should be reported together with resampling-based stability estimates.

title: PIU Smart Intelligence Agents: Design and Implementation of a Security-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture for Enterprise Intelligence
abstract: Enterprises increasingly rely on heterogeneous documents, relational databases, and analytical systems to support information retrieval and business decision-making. Integrating large language models (LLMs) with these sources introduces challenges in evidence reliability, analytical correctness, access control, and operational resilience. This paper presents PIU Smart Intelligence Agents, a security-aware multi-agent architecture designed to integrate enterprise document intelligence, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, document summarization, naturallanguage-to-SQL analytics, key performance indicator (KPI) generation, and conversational AI within a common application and governance framework. The proposed architecture organizes specialized AI capabilities around shared services for authentication, authorization, request validation, provider integration, observability, and controlled data access. Its document-processing workflow encompasses file validation, text extraction, optical character recognition for scanned documents, normalization, chunking, embedding generation, and vector-based indexing. The structured-analytics workflow separates schema-aware query generation from SQL validation, restricted database execution, and result interpretation. The architecture also addresses provider compatibility, timeout handling, failure recovery, document lifecycle management, and traceability of generated outputs. The source implementation reports 1,242 automated tests passed and two integration tests skipped. These results are reported implementation evidence and have not been independently reproduced. The available evidence does not establish comprehensive external RAG benchmark performance, quantitative correctness across all agents, independently validated security effectiveness, or production-scale performance and recovery guarantees. Accordingly, this study presents an integrated engineering architecture and identifies a reproducible evaluation framework for assessing its effectiveness. The principal contribution is the systematic integration of heterogeneous enterprise AI capabilities with explicit governance and validation requirements, rather than the introduction of a new learning or retrieval algorithm. Future work should prioritize agent-specific correctness testing, retrieval and answer-quality benchmarks, adversarial security evaluation, controlled load testing, and recovery verification.

title: Adaptive MIMO fuzzy PID controller based on Runge-Kutta model
abstract: Nonlinear multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems are difficult to control because of input–output coupling, measurement noise, and parameter variations. This study proposes a Runge–Kutta (RK) model-based predictive adaptive MIMO fuzzy proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller for nonlinear dynamical systems. A fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) model predicts future outputs and provides the sensitivity information required to update the fuzzy PID scaling parameters online using the Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) algorithm. An additive correction mechanism provides supplementary control action during transient conditions and plant–model mismatch. Furthermore, a discrete-time Lyapunov-based stability analysis is established, guaranteeing the uniform ultimate boundedness (UUB) of the tracking errors and the boundedness of adaptive parameters under aggregate disturbances. The proposed controller is evaluated on a nonlinear three-tank system under nominal conditions, measurement noise, and time-varying parametric uncertainty. For comparative evaluation, an existing RK model-based adaptive MIMO PID controller is employed as a benchmark under the same operating scenarios. Both controllers maintain bounded tracking responses, control inputs, and adaptive parameters. The composite performance-index values obtained with the proposed fuzzy PID controller are 0.2660, 0.2701, and 1.0739, corresponding to improvements of 6.11%, 6.12%, and 3.59%, respectively, over the benchmark controller. In the parametric-uncertainty case, the RK-based parameter estimator follows the variations in the uncertain inter-tank flow coefficient and reduces the resulting plant–model mismatch. Although the benchmark adaptive PID controller has lower computational requirements, the average and maximum cycle times of both controllers remain substantially below the sampling period. The results demonstrate that the proposed adaptive MIMO fuzzy PID controller improves the combined tracking and control-variation performance while retaining computational feasibility.
